{
 "summary": "Updates `HTTPRemoteClient::m_keep_alive` under `m_send_mutex` when appending replies rather than before acquiring the lock, and switches the field from `std::atomic_bool` to `bool GUARDED_BY(m_send_mutex)`. A unit test using a mock socket is added to deterministically exercise pipelined request handling.",
 "problem": "Because `m_keep_alive` was set before acquiring the send buffer lock, an I/O thread draining a pipelined keep-alive response could observe an empty buffer alongside a freshly cleared keep-alive flag from a subsequent `Connection: close` request before that second response was actually queued. The I/O thread would then flag the connection for closure, dropping the queued second response.",
 "evidence": [
  "The author notes the bug is low-severity because the race window is narrow and `bitcoin-cli` does not pipeline requests (PR description).",
  "A new unit test reproduces the bug deterministically, failing without the fix with `server.GetConnectionsCount() == 1 has failed [0 != 1]` when the client is prematurely disconnected with data remaining in its buffer (PR description)."

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
